



         On the abundance of finite p-groups.  *



                         A. Jaikin-Zapirain

                Departamento de Matem'aticas-Matematika Saila

                    Facultad de Ciencias-Zientzi Fakultatea

             Universidad del Pa'is Vasco-Euskal Herriko Unibertsitatea

                      Apdo. 644,  48080-Bilbao, Spain



                            May 4, 2000



                              Abstract

        In this paper we prove that there are only finitely many p-groups of
     any given abundance. This result gives a positive answer to a problem
     raised by Shalev in [6]. We also prove that the cobreadth of a p-group
     can be bounded by a function which depends only on the abundance of
     the group (and not on p).



1    Introduction


Let G be a finite p-group and let r(G) denote the number of conjugacy classes
of G.  By a result of P. Hall (for example, see [2, Chapter 5, Theorem 15.2])
if |G| = pm and m = 2n + e, where e = 0, 1, then there exists a non-negative
integer a = a(G), which we call the abundance of G, such that

                   r(G) = pe + (p2 - 1)(n + a(p - 1)).

In [5] Poland proved that if a = 0 then G is a group of maximal class whose
order is at most pp+2.  This bound is exact for p # 7.  For p # 11 the exact
bound was found in [1] and is pp+1.

   In this work we consider finite p-groups with arbitrary abundance and prove
the following result.

Theorem 1.1.   There are only finitely many p-groups of any given abundance.


   Set rkG = max {d(H) | H # G}, where d(H) is the minimum number of
generators of the subgroup H. Then from [6, Proposition 4.8] we know that there
____________________________*

 *try and
by the DGICYT Grant PB97-0604.

is a number l = l(rkG) > 0 which depends only on rkG such that r(G) # |G|l.
Therefore in order to prove Theorem 1.1 it suffices to show that rkG is (p, a)-
bounded. In this paper we say that a certain invariant is (p, a)-bounded if it *
 *is
bounded above by some function of (p, a). Let i # 1 and |#i(G)/#i+1(G)| = pk.
By using Hall's formula and bearing in mind that the abundance of G/#i+1(G)
is less than or equal to that of G, we obtain


    pk - 1 # r(G/#i+1(G)) - r(G/#i(G)) # (p2 - 1)((k + 1)/2 + a(p - 1)).


Hence, it is clear now that the order of #i(G)/#i+1(G) is (p, a)-bounded for any
i # 1. In particular, d(G) is (p, a)-bounded.

   Recall that a finite p-group H is powerful if p is odd and H/Hp is abelian,
or p = 2 and H/H4 is abelian.  Throughout this paper we shall use various
facts about powerful p-groups, which can be found in [4]. For example, if H is a
powerful p-group then rkH = d(H). By using this equality it is not difficult to
see that in order to bound rkG it suffices to prove the existence of a powerful
subgroup of (p, a)-bounded index. Therefore Theorem 1.1 follows from the next
results.
                                                                         s-p-2
Theorem 1.2.   Let p be an odd prime and G a finite p-group. If a(G) < 2p_____p*
 *2-1
then #ps(G) is powerful.

Theorem 1.3.   Let G be a finite 2-group. If a(G) < 2s-1 - 1 then #2s(G)2 is
powerful.


   Refining this argument we obtain the following quantitative version of The-
orem 1.1.

Theorem 1.4.   There is a function h = h(a), such that for any p-group G of
order pm and abundance a, the inequality m # h . p6 holds.


   Let x # G and define cb(x) = logp|CG (x)|.  Then the cobreadth of G is
cb(G) = minx#G cb(x). If G is a p-group of maximal class then cb(G) = 2, and
so a(G) = 0 implies cb(G) # 2.  Using Theorem 1.4 we shall prove that the
cobreadth can be bounded by a function which depends only on the abundance
(and not on p).

   In the following, if T # G then rG (T ) is the number of conjugacy classes in
G whose intersection with T is not empty.

   In the next section we prove Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3.  Section 3 is
devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.4.



2    Proof of the main result


For the rest of this paper, we assume that the group G satisfies the hypotheses
of Theorems 1.2 or 1.3. First we prove that d(#ps(G)) # ps. Note that by [4,



                                  2




Proposition 1.13] this inequality proves Theorem 1.2. Suppose that d(#ps(G)) >
ps. Then there exists a normal subgroupsN of G such that K = #ps(G)/N is
an elementary abelian group of order pp +1. Put H = G/N. Since the group H
acts on K, we have a homomorphism


                        #: H -> GL(ps + 1, Fp).


Suppose that x # H and o(#(x)) = pk. If we consider the Jordan form of #(x)
we obtain that |CK (x)| # p(ps/pk)+1for 0 # k # s and |CK (x)| # p for k # s+1
([3, Corollary 2.6]). Hence


                      |CH (x)| # |CK (x)|pk # ps+2.


Let c be the nilpotency class of H. It is clear that c # 2ps. Choose T1 # H
such that |H :T1| = p2 and #2(H) # T1 and put Ti = #i(H) for 2 # i # c + 1.
For i # 1 define
                   ci= |{1 # k # c | |Tk: Tk+1| = pi}|.

                      (p2 - 1)a # m - 2 - (p + 1).

3     The relation between the abundance and the

     cobreadth


Proof of Theorem 1.4.Without loss of generality we mayssuppose that p is odd.
Let s be the smalest integer satisfying a = a(G) < 2p_-p-2_p2-1. Put H = #ps(G)

and ~G= G/H. From the proof of Theorem 1.2 we know that d(H) # ps and
H is powerful. Let |G~| = pm1 and |H| = pm2 . First we shall analyze m1. If we
put di= |{1 # k # ps - 1 | |#k(G~)/#k+1(G~)| = pi}|, we obtain

                          X         X
                     m1 =    idi,      di# ps - 1.
                           i         i

Hence we have
           X                  X
  r(G~) #     di(pi- 1) + 1 #    di(pi- 1 + p2 - 1) + 1 - (ps - 1)(p2 - 1)
           Xi                  i

        #     idi(p2 - 1) + 1 - (ps - 1)(p2 - 1)
            i
        =  (m1 + 1)(p2 - 1) - ps(p2 - 1) + 1.


On the other hand,


            r(G~) #  (m1 + 1)(p2 - 1)/2 + (p - 1)(p2 - 1)a

                  #  (m1 + 1)(p2 - 1)/2 + (p - 1)(2ps - p - 2)



                                  5




and we obtain the following inequality for m1,

         (m1 + 1)(p2 - 1)/2 # ps(p2 - 1) + (p - 1)(2ps - p - 2) - 1.

Now, it is not dificult to see that m1 # 3ps.

   Since H is powerful, we know from [6, Lemma 4.7] that r(H) # p-1_p|H|1/d(H).
Hence

                                                      s          m /ps-3ps-1
        rG (H) # ___1___|Gr:(H|H) # _p_-_1_p3ps+1pm2/p = (p - 1)p 2        .


By Hall's formula

    rG (H)  #  r(G) - r(G~) + 1 # (m2 + 1)(p2 - 1)/2 + (p - 1)(p2 - 1)a

            #  (m2 + 1)(p2 - 1)/2 + (p - 1)(2ps - p - 2).

If we compare these two inequalities for rG (H) we obtain
                  s-3ps-1                        s
             pm2/p       # (m2 + 1)(p + 1)/2 + 2p  - p - 2.

Now, writing m2 = cp2s and analyzing c, we see that m2 # 5p2s.
                                                s-1-p-2
   We have chosen the integer s such that a # 2p_______p2-1.  Therefore ps #

(a + 1)p3. Hence m = m1 + m2 # 3ps + 5p2s # 3(a + 1)p3 + 5(a + 1)2p6, and
the proof is finished.

Corollary 3.1. The cobreadth of a p-group G is bounded above in terms of its
abundance only.


Proof. From the previous theorem and Hall's formula we obtain that there exists
f = f(a) such that r(G) # f(a)p8. On the other hand

                             X   |CG (x)|
                      r(G) =     _______# pcbG.
                             x#G   |G|

Hence cbG # 8 + logpf(a). In particular, cbG # 8 + log2f(a).            |___|
